ABOUT: This is the fourth edition of an independent reading of The Real Eisman Playbook, the podcast Steve Eisman has published every week since June 2025. It covers all 152 episodes to 25 September 2026, including the 19 released only to paid Substack subscribers, and more than a million words of transcript.

The earlier editions were reports. This one is built to be used. It opens with the playbook on one page, gives every chapter a short summary, and adds four chapters that turn the analysis into tools: his stock checklist and red flags, his rules sector by sector, the frameworks he reuses, and a dated ledger of his positions, calls and tripwires. A reading list, a glossary and a guest bench grouped by subject close the book, and MLow's fifty Eisman method posters illustrate the rules throughout.
ABOUT_METHOD: Every episode was transcribed by machine and read in full. Synopses and dossiers were written from those transcripts and checked against them. Quotations are kept short, dated and attributed; because the transcripts are automated, check the wording against the audio before quoting any of them in public.

Positions and thresholds move. Every position in this book carries the date he stated it, and the ledger in Chapter 23 is current to 25 September 2026. Treat anything later as unknown until you have checked a newer episode.
This is analysis of a public figure's published views, not investment advice, and it is not affiliated with Steve Eisman or The Real Eisman Playbook.
READING_PATHS: The playbook on one page, then Chapter 3 for the sentence the show hangs on, then the ledger in Chapter 23 for where he stands today.
Part III in order: the rules, the stock lens, the sector playbooks and the frameworks. Then his portfolio in Chapter 22 and the ledger in Chapter 23.
If you are new to the show
Appendix A lists sixteen episodes worth hearing first. Read Part I alongside them, then Part II for the arguments the episodes keep returning to.
Appendices B and C hold a synopsis of every episode and a dossier for every interview and lecture. Chapter 26 lists the questions they leave open.
ONE_PAGE: One sentence carries the show.

On 9 January 2026 he said the market might power through a weak economy as long as AI trends hold, and that if they falter he would expect an enormous correction. Nearly every other position follows from it.
The economy is K-shaped, and AI is most of the growth.

US GDP grew by about 500 billion dollars in 2025 while AI capital spending ran above 400 billion. Strip it out and growth rounds to nothing. He is careful to add that this alone does not cause a recession.
On AI he refuses the bubble call but has moved a long way.

From calling the story still in its infancy in June 2025, to selling Alphabet, Meta and Oracle by July 2026, to naming OpenAI the US economy's Achilles heel in September. He keeps four questions apart that most people merge.
His most important new rule is about capital.

Software used to be capital light. When the hyperscalers began asking shareholders to fund their spending, he sold them and moved toward power, chips and equipment companies that will not need to raise money.
Private credit converted him once the data arrived.

He refused to call it a bubble without data, then became the house bear when redemption gates supplied it. He expects real losses through software borrowers, with refinancings due from 2027, but not a repeat of 2008.
The man who shorted the banks says they are safe.
Post-crisis rules more than halved their leverage. In 2026 he dropped his own idea that bank credit leads the economy, because the economy now hinges on AI.
He forecasts mechanisms, not dates.
A bear case a year early is indistinguishable from a wrong one, so he accepts a guest's direction and refuses the clock. Asked for the next black swan, he says the question misunderstands the term.
He books his own opposition.
An alarming guest is followed by the credible opposite, and he says on air which way he moved. The limit: when he already agrees, nobody argues the other side.
He keeps score on himself, in public.
Charter was recommended, defended, then sold with a plain admission of error. His 4.5% line on the ten-year yield was retired the moment the market proved it wrong.
The book, as of September 2026.

Fifteen of the sixteen longs he disclosed in July, after selling Charter; shorts in FICO and Trupanion; the largest gains partly hedged; and the ten-year line moved to 5%, above which he calls a correction probably imminent.

IN_BRIEF.show: The podcast runs on a strict weekly rhythm: a Monday interview that takes one expert through one sector, and a Friday wrap where his own views run undiluted. Lectures, panels and reaction episodes sit on top.
IN_BRIEF.who: Nearly every framework he teaches comes from a specific career stop: subprime coverage at Oppenheimer, the FrontPoint years of The Big Short, and a decade at Neuberger Berman. The podcast is what he built after leaving institutions in 2024.
IN_BRIEF.frame: Twice a year he writes his thinking down and then holds himself to it: four themes for 2025 and five structural themes for 2026. One sentence from 9 January 2026 carries the whole show.
IN_BRIEF.arc: Read in order, the 152 episodes tell one story: a market that began by celebrating AI capital spending and ended by auditing it. The arc runs through a war, a private credit panic and his own cancer treatment without a missed week.
IN_BRIEF.k: Strip AI capital spending out of 2025's GDP growth and almost nothing is left. The phrase organises the show from October 2025, but he is careful about its limits: on its own it does not produce a recession.
IN_BRIEF.ai: The most covered subject, and the one where his position visibly moves: from a story still in its infancy in June 2025 to selling three AI names by July 2026 and calling OpenAI the economy's Achilles heel in September. He still will not call it a bubble.
IN_BRIEF.pc: He began as the sceptic of the sceptics because no data existed, and became the house bear once redemption gates supplied it. He expects real losses through software borrowers, but not a 2008-style collapse.
IN_BRIEF.afford: Housing is a local supply problem, not a demand problem, and he says politicians keep reaching for the wrong fix. He still buys homebuilders at or below tangible book, and owns Meritage Homes.
IN_BRIEF.banks: The man who shorted the banks into 2008 says they are safe, because post-crisis rules more than halved their leverage. In 2026 he dropped two of his own bank ideas: that bank credit leads the economy, and that regional mergers make a trade.
IN_BRIEF.crypto: His critique is narrow and repeated: Bitcoin falls with tech stocks on fearful days, which contradicts its own thesis. Stablecoins interest him as payments, but he thinks only Visa and Mastercard hold real franchises.
IN_BRIEF.method: Twelve operating rules, stated across the wraps and lectures: buy market power, write down your falsifiers, read the balance sheet, pay for data nobody else buys, and never mistake two correlated bets for a hedge. Each rule has its own posters in Part VI.
IN_BRIEF.stocklens: The rules in Chapter 11, turned into the order he actually applies them: eight questions for a long, the red flags that end the conversation, how he sells, and the nine verdicts he lands on.
IN_BRIEF.sectors: He has no single way to value a stock. Each sector is valued on terms its investors agree, and he has a short playbook for each one he covers.
IN_BRIEF.frameworks: The mental models he applies to every new risk, named the way he names them on air, with the date each is stated most clearly.
IN_BRIEF.short: Two July 2025 episodes with professional short sellers produced the show's most practical rules: never short a cult, never short on valuation alone, and expect three to five painful rallies on the way down.
IN_BRIEF.gfc: His model of 2008 has four causes: leverage, a blown-up asset class, systemic institutions owning it, and derivatives. He uses it as a test for every new worry, and private credit fails it.
IN_BRIEF.class: Read together, the lessons from every episode form a short course in four parts: reading markets, credit, valuation, and behaviour. Each lesson traces to several dated episodes.
IN_BRIEF.teachers: The guest list looks like a parade of analysts, but he uses it deliberately: he books his own opposition, stages second opinions and runs investigations across several episodes.
IN_BRIEF.second: Booking the credible opposite of an alarming guest is a repeatable procedure with a fixed shape. It has one honest limit: when he already agrees with a guest, nobody argues the other side.
IN_BRIEF.minds: He updates often but along strict lines: he adopts frameworks readily, accepts timing calls almost never, and turns more negative when a company's numbers cannot be checked.
IN_BRIEF.mistakes: He keeps score on himself in public. Charter was recommended, defended, then sold with a plain admission of error, and his 4.5% line on the ten-year was retired when the market proved it wrong.
IN_BRIEF.portfolio: On 1 July 2026 he disclosed his whole book: 16 longs in five themes, two shorts, and three AI names sold because they started asking shareholders to fund capital spending. In September he hedged his largest gains without selling them.
IN_BRIEF.ledger: Where he stands on every subject the show covers, what would change his mind, and the numbers he watches, each with the date he said it.
IN_BRIEF.substack: The 19 subscriber-only episodes are where he is least hedged: the full portfolio, A Conspiracy of Credit, the bank lectures and the hardest AI bear. They are the most useful material in the corpus and the most dated.
IN_BRIEF.outside: His record before the podcast explains its moral register: Subprime Goes to College in 2010, years of television, and a careful distance from The Big Short legend.
IN_BRIEF.openq: Four arguments the show has framed carefully and cannot yet close: AI returns, private credit, the consumer and his own thresholds. Each now carries a dated test worth holding him to.
IN_BRIEF.nuggets: Lines that fit no single chapter but recur, or are simply the most useful sentences in the corpus.

STOCKLENS.title: The stock lens
intro: He is a stock picker, not a trader. He finds a story with a compelling thesis, checks it every quarter and between quarters, takes a full position at once rather than leveraging in, and sells when the thesis breaks rather than when the price moves. He prefers growth stories, owns a turnaround only when it is priced as if it will go bankrupt, and invests only in the United States.
quote: If I think I'm right, I take a full position without leveraging up slowly. If I'm wrong, I sell.
checklist: Is there a story, and can you state it in a sentence?
Investors love stories; without one nobody cares, which is why wireless and cable languish whatever their cash flow.
Proprietary products, duopolies, pricing power. Proprietary data beats AI disruption, and in a broken industry the survivor is the cost leader, not the best story.
His most important change of 2026. Prefer companies that will not have to raise money; it is why he sold Alphabet, Meta and Oracle and owns Nvidia, Arista, Apple and three power names.
What does the balance sheet say?
It matters as much as the income statement, and sometimes more. A free cash flow yield above 20% says the market suspects bankruptcy; when the balance sheet disagrees, that gap is the opportunity.

It is always the management. Growth in tangible book per share over ten to fifteen years is the scoreboard that survives cycles, and a turnaround chief executive who declares everything fixed is telling you it has not started.
He hardens fastest when a company cannot answer a disclosure question. Without better disclosure a stock is very hard to recommend at any valuation.
Is the cycle behind you or against you?
Stock picking works best when the macro is neutral or helping. Fighting rising rates in rate-sensitive groups is hopeless.
Write the falsifiers down before buying. Thesis creep, rewriting the reason as the stock moves, is the bane of every investor.

Taxes are the hidden factor. He would rather hold a winner than pay the gain, and hedges instead.

SECTORS.title: Sector by sector
intro: He distrusts discounted cash flow because it needs too many variables. How a sector is valued is set by consensus, which he calls the mafia, and arguing that a whole sector is mispriced is a waste of time. Accept the terms of the debate or do not play.
valuation: Expensive is acceptable with a long backlog. Orders that fill over years give visibility a multiple cannot see.
At perfection multiples, around 40 to 47 times earnings, beating is table stakes and only raised guidance holds the stock.
Cheap is not the test. An improving story beats a cheap broken one, and in software cheapness is a symptom.
A business whose earnings track short-term rates does not deserve a technology multiple. Stablecoin issuers are asset managers.
A quality franchise going sideways is a valuation reset in disguise.
After a run of 100% to 300%, the question shifts from the story to how much multiple expansion is left.
playbooks: Banks
The one business where the cost of goods, loan losses, is unknown at the point of sale.
Return on tangible common equity sets the price to tangible book, and valuations move within a range.
Deposits are only as stable as they are diverse. Funding long bonds with short money can fail a bank without one bad loan, as at Silicon Valley Bank.
Buy after recession fears have crushed them; lighten up at peak valuations. Stick to the large banks.
Watch non-accruals at the four biggest banks for the broadest read on credit.
Homebuilders
Buy at or below tangible book while profitable, because profits compound book.
Rate sensitive with no escape. Incentives and rate buy-downs protect volume and destroy margin.
They move before the fundamentals confirm, so if they work, they work early.
Insurance
Property and casualty runs its own cycle, not the economy's: the safe corner of financials.
Life insurers trade at three to five times earnings because of decades of long-tail blowups, and buybacks beat acquisitions at that price.
Private-equity-owned insurers buying their parent's paper have no arm's-length pricing and hidden offshore leverage.
Payments
Only Visa and Mastercard are long-term investments; everything else is a trade.
A new payment rail must beat the incumbent on the whole job, win both sides of the market and match fraud protection.
Visa is as good a single read on the consumer as any company that reports.
Software
Model it as seats times price per seat. AI threatens both at once.
Treat the group as impaired until the data says otherwise. He will not buy until he knows how far growth estimates fall when the cost of writing software collapses.
For software credit: no moat, no proprietary data, and quickly installed means quickly replaced.
AI and semiconductors
Follow the bottlenecks. In a supply-constrained boom, investors chase whatever is scarce.
When an industry turns capital intensive, look for the supplier that owns the pricing power.
The binding constraint on AI is physical: power, turbines, transformers, permits and skilled labour.
Energy and cyclicals
Buy when the commodity has collapsed and nobody will touch them; sell when everyone is excited. They are value and trading vehicles, not growth holdings.
Biotech
Better science is not a better business. Ask what the endpoint is first.
Early trial data is a filtered sample; Phase 3 removes the curation.
Where the exit is an acquisition, ask whether a large buyer will want it.
Defence
The primes are too big to pivot, and budget flows to nimble newcomers. Aftermarket nuclear is the quiet compounder.
When the rules change
Ask what a company can do tomorrow that it could not do yesterday. When a regulatory cage opens, the low-cost producer captures the most.
A listing that institutions cannot legally buy carries a discount that disappears when they can.

FRAMEWORKS.title: The frameworks he reuses
FRAMEWORKS.intro: He names his tools on air and reuses them on every new risk. These are the ones that recur most, with the moves he makes when he frames a story.
items: From the 2008 lectures: too much leverage, a large asset class blowing up, systemic institutions owning it, and derivatives tying balance sheets together. The first three appear in almost every crisis. For any new worry, ask whether all three are present. Private credit fails the test, so he expects losses, not collapse.
Credit problems emerge where the growth was
Subprime before 2008; private credit and AI data centre debt now. Prosperity itself degrades underwriting, so look hardest where lending grew fastest.

He will not call a bubble without data. In 2006 he read the Moody's securitisation database every month like a Rosetta Stone. Private credit has no equivalent, which is why opacity itself became his worry: small unknown losses panic everyone who might hold the bag.
Every industry has one constraint that governs everything else. For large banks it is the stress capital buffer; for AI it is physical power. Find it before forecasting anything.
Split each earnings season into AI and everything else. The K-shape shows up in earnings before it reaches the macro data.
The first leg down is often public relations noise. The second, on a fundamental miss, is not.
Read the reaction, not the headline
A beat that sinks the stock means the category is being repriced, not the quarter. Watch what investors punish, not what companies report.
Name the rhyme, then its limit
1929 was credit plus leverage plus fear of missing out; 2008 had four causes. Name the historical rhyme, then say why this time differs.
Regulation: never whether, only how much
Unregulated capitalism runs to booms and busts; too much regulation kills the golden goose. There is no formula, only iteration, and regulatory capture is real but cyclical.
The hardest thing a person lives through. The MLP investors, the 1929 bankers and the pre-2008 executives each held a paradigm that stopped being true before they stopped believing it.

Seasonal patterns persist because people's reactions change more slowly than the news, but a pattern is never a signal on its own. The market is his favourite economist, and he keeps a graveyard for dead indicators as well as dead stocks.
He forecasts mechanisms, not timing. Every serious call carries a falsifier or a clock instead.

GLOSSARY: Beta
How much a stock tends to move when the market moves. His preferred measure of portfolio risk, in place of stress-test scenarios.
Binding constraint
The one limit that governs everything else in an industry. See Chapter 14.
Business development company (BDC)
A fund that lends to private companies. Non-traded BDCs sell to individuals and allow only limited redemptions each quarter.
Capex
Capital expenditure: money spent on long-lived assets such as data centres, chips and power plants.
Collateralised debt obligation (CDO)
A security built from pools of other debt, often the riskier slices of mortgage bonds. Central to 2008.
Constructive sale
A tax rule that treats certain hedges of a winning position, such as shorting against the box, as if the shares had been sold.
Credit default swap (CDS)
A contract that pays out if a borrower or bond defaults. His instrument for the Big Short trades.
Equal-weight index
A version of the S&P 500 in which every company counts the same. Its gap with the ordinary index measures how narrow the market is.
Falsifier
The evidence that would prove a thesis wrong, written down before buying.
Free cash flow yield
Free cash flow divided by market value. Above 20%, he reads it as the market suspecting bankruptcy.
Gate
A fund limiting withdrawals, usually to 5% of assets a quarter, when too many investors ask for their money at once.
Hyperscaler
One of the largest cloud companies: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle.
K-shaped economy
An economy where one group of companies and households pulls ahead while another falls behind. See Chapter 5.
Non-accrual loan
A loan on which a bank has stopped booking interest because repayment is in doubt.
Private credit
Loans made directly to companies by funds rather than banks, mostly to companies owned by private equity.
Risk-weighted assets
A bank's assets scaled by regulatory risk weights. Capital ratios divide by these rather than by total assets, which he blames for the leverage of 2008.
SaaSpocalypse
The 2026 sell-off in software stocks on fears that AI erodes both the number of seats and the price per seat.
Secular decline
Long-term structural shrinkage, as opposed to a cyclical dip. The most durable kind of short.
Shorting against the box
Shorting a stock you already own, to lock in a gain without selling.
Special purpose vehicle (SPV)
A separate company set up to hold assets or debt, often keeping them off the parent's balance sheet.
Stablecoin
A token pegged to the dollar and backed mainly by Treasury bills. To him, a payments question, not a cryptocurrency.
Stress capital buffer
The extra capital the Fed's annual stress test requires of large banks. The binding constraint on them.
Tangible book value
A company's equity minus goodwill and other intangibles. Banks and homebuilders are valued against it.
Ten-year yield
The interest rate on ten-year US Treasury notes. His threshold for the stock market, now 5%.
Thesis creep
Quietly rewriting the reason you own a stock as its price moves. The failure he warns about most.
Tranche
A slice of a securitisation with its own rank for absorbing losses. BBB-minus sits near the bottom.
